draft.title: Integrals of exponential and trig functions
card: Each rule comes from reversing a derivative. ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C. ∫cos x dx = sin x + C. ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C.
Watch the sign for sine: ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, because the derivative of cos x is −sin x.
If the inside is linear, ax + b, divide by a. ∫e^(ax+b) dx = e^(ax+b) ÷ a + C. ∫cos(ax+b) dx = sin(ax+b) ÷ a + C. The same works for sin and sec².
Example: ∫e³ˣ dx = e³ˣ/3 + C. Check by differentiating: the derivative of e³ˣ/3 is 3e³ˣ/3 = e³ˣ.
draft.remember: Integrate the function, then divide by the number in front of x. Sine gives −cos.

a.why: The derivative of −cos x is sin x, so −cos x + C is the integral. cos x + C is tempting, but its derivative is −sin x, which has the wrong sign.
a.clue: Differentiate your answer and see if you get sin x.

b.why: Divide by the 2 in front of x, so the integral is sin(2x)/2 + C. Differentiating gives 2cos(2x)/2 = cos(2x). Multiplying by 2 instead is a common slip, and sin(2x) + C would differentiate to 2cos(2x).
b.clue: Differentiating sin(2x) brings out an extra factor. Cancel it.

final.title: Integrals of exponential and trig functions
card: Each rule comes from reversing a derivative. \(\int e^{x} \, dx = e^{x} + C\). \(\int \cos x \, dx = \sin x + C\). \(\int \sec^{2} x \, dx = \tan x + C\).
Watch the sign for sine: \(\int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + C\), because the derivative of \(\cos x\) is \(-\sin x\).

If the inside is linear, \(ax + b\), divide by \(a\). \(\int e^{ax + b} \, dx = \frac{e^{ax + b}}{a} + C\). \(\int \cos(ax + b) \, dx = \frac{\sin(ax + b)}{a} + C\). The same works for \(\sin\) and \(\sec^{2}\).
Example: \(\int e^{3x} \, dx = \frac{e^{3x}}{3} + C\). Check by differentiating: the derivative of \(\frac{e^{3x}}{3}\) is \(\frac{3e^{3x}}{3} = e^{3x}\).
final.remember: Integrate the function, then divide by the number in front of \(x\). Sine gives \(-\cos\).

a.why: The derivative of \(-\cos x\) is \(\sin x\), so \(-\cos x + C\) is the integral. \(\cos x + C\) is tempting, but its derivative is \(-\sin x\), which has the wrong sign.
a.clue: Differentiate your answer and see if you get \(\sin x\).

b.why: Divide by the 2 in front of \(x\), so the integral is \(\frac{\sin(2x)}{2} + C\). Differentiating gives \(\frac{2\cos(2x)}{2} = \cos(2x)\). Multiplying by 2 instead is a common slip, and \(\sin(2x) + C\) would differentiate to \(2\cos(2x)\).
b.clue: Differentiating \(\sin(2x)\) brings out an extra factor. Cancel it.
